h:
In November 2026, an international religious movement plans to gather in Jerusalem under the banner of the Seven Laws of Noah. Its organizers speak of biblical prophecy, the nations returning to God, and the establishment of a new religious authority.

The commandments themselves will sound familiar to anyone who has read Scripture. Their origins, however, lead us through Genesis, the Book of Jubilees, and centuries of rabbinic interpretation.

To understand what is now being organized in Jerusalem, we must first establish what God commanded, what the rabbis developed, and where the two meet.

What Are the Seven Laws of Noah?

After the Flood, Noah stepped into a world that had been washed of its violence. The earth was no longer filled with the generations that had corrupted it. His family stood at the beginning of another human age, and God established a covenant that would extend far beyond the eight people who had survived aboard the ark.

Thousands of years later, that covenant has become the foundation of an international religious movement.

From November 2-6, 2026, the Noahide World Center plans to gather delegates from six continents in Jerusalem for what it calls the First International Congress of Noahides. Its organizers intend to establish a founding charter, regional councils, a unified religious syllabus, and an international Beit Din, a rabbinic court.

They have chosen the Mount of Olives as their gathering place, overlooking Jerusalem and the Temple Mount. They have also chosen a passage from the prophet Zechariah to explain the significance of their meeting.

The prophecy speaks of many nations joining themselves to the Lord.

The organizers follow it with a declaration of their own:

“This is that day.”

Before examining what they intend to establish, we need to understand the religious foundation beneath it.

What exactly are the Seven Laws of Noah? Where did they come from? And what relationship do they have to the covenant God actually established in Scripture?

The answer begins in Genesis.

What God Actually Commanded Noah

God established His covenant with Noah long before the emergence of rabbinic Judaism. Scripture tells us exactly what He commanded.

When Noah and his family emerge from the ark, God blesses them and commands them to multiply upon the earth, forbids the consumption of blood, and establishes the sanctity of human life, declaring that man was made in His image.

Genesis 9:4-6:

“But flesh with blood of life ye shall not eat. For your blood of your lives will I require a recompense; from the hand of all wild beasts will I require it, and from the hand of man his brother will I require the life of man. He that sheds man’s blood, instead of that blood shall his own be shed, for in the image of God I made man.”

The passage establishes two important principles. Life belongs to God, and man bears His image. The shedding of innocent human blood is therefore a matter of divine judgment.

God then announces the covenant itself.

“And I, behold, I establish my covenant with you, and with your seed after you.”- Genesis 9:9

The covenant extends beyond Noah’s immediate family. God includes their descendants and the living creatures of the earth. He promises that all flesh will never again be destroyed by a flood, and the rainbow becomes the visible sign of that promise.

This is the covenant recorded in Scripture.

Yet nowhere in Genesis 9 does God present Noah with a numbered collection of seven laws.

The distinction matters because the familiar Seven Noahide Laws contain commandments drawn from several parts of Scripture, not simply from God’s words to Noah after the Flood.

Those seven laws, as taught in rabbinic Judaism, are:

  • The prohibition of idolatry.
  • The prohibition of blaspheming God.
  • The prohibition of murder.
  • The prohibition of forbidden sexual relations.
  • The prohibition of theft.
  • The prohibition of eating flesh taken from a living animal.
  • The obligation to establish courts of justice.

Christians will recognize the moral substance of much of this list. Scripture repeatedly condemns murder, theft, sexual immorality, and idolatry. God commands justice, and Genesis establishes the sacredness of human life.

So the question is not whether these moral principles appear in Scripture. They do.

The question is how they became a distinct religious code for the nations, administered through the interpretations and authority of Jewish sages.

For that, we must examine the rabbinic records.

How the Rabbis Built the Seven-Law Framework

The Seven Noahide Laws are commonly associated with the Babylonian Talmud, particularly tractate Sanhedrin 56a.

There, the rabbis preserve a teaching that the descendants of Noah were commanded concerning seven matters: courts of justice, blasphemy, idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, bloodshed, robbery, and eating a limb from a living animal.

The passage presents the seven commandments as obligations imposed upon the descendants of Noah, meaning humanity generally.

But the tradition did not originate with the completed Babylonian Talmud.

An earlier rabbinic collection, the Tosefta, also preserves a seven-commandment tradition in Avodah Zarah 8:4. The Tosefta belongs to the early centuries of rabbinic Judaism, while the Babylonian Talmud reached its developed form centuries later.

This is important for understanding the history accurately. The Talmud preserves and develops an earlier rabbinic tradition; it did not invent all seven commandments.

The more revealing detail is how the rabbis establish their biblical basis.

In Sanhedrin 56b, the discussion turns to Genesis 2:16, where God commands Adam concerning the trees of the garden.

The rabbis interpret individual expressions within that verse as references to separate legal obligations. Through this method, they derive commandments concerning courts, God’s name, idolatry, sexual relations, theft, and other matters.

They also discuss additional prohibitions and alternative enumerations. Some rabbinic authorities include restrictions concerning castration, sorcery, or mixing different kinds of animals and plants.

This tells us something significant about the formation of the Noahide system.

The rabbis were not simply copying a seven-point list spoken by God to Noah in Genesis. They were interpreting earlier passages, combining commandments, and constructing a legal classification for humanity.

The underlying moral commands were ancient. The formal system belonged to rabbinic interpretation.

There is another ancient witness worth examining.

The Book of Jubilees, preserved within the Ethiopian biblical canon, gives us an earlier account of Noah’s instructions to his descendants.

“And in the twenty-eighth jubilee Noah began to enjoin upon his sons’ sons the ordinances and commandments, and all the judgments that he knew, and he exhorted his sons to observe righteousness, and to cover the shame of their flesh, and to bless their Creator, and honour father and mother, and love their neighbour, and guard their souls from fornication and uncleanness and all iniquity.” - Jubilees 7:20

The following verses recount the corruption that brought judgment upon the generations before the Flood. Noah warns his descendants against sexual immorality, violence, and bloodshed, reminding them of the destruction their ancestors brought upon themselves.

Notice the breadth of his instruction. Noah commands his descendants to honor their parents, love their neighbors, bless their Creator, and practice righteousness. These obligations extend beyond the familiar seven commandments later enumerated by the rabbis.

Jubilees therefore preserves a scriptural account of Noah’s teachings that predates the surviving rabbinic compilations. The moral obligations are already present, but they are not arranged into the formal seven-law system subsequently developed in rabbinic Judaism.

We can now trace the development through three distinct sources. Genesis records God’s covenant with Noah and his descendants. Jubilees preserves Noah’s instructions concerning righteousness and the conduct of future generations. Rabbinic literature takes these ancient commandments and organizes them into a defined legal framework of seven obligations for humanity.

The distinction is important. The moral commandments have their foundations in Scripture, while the seven-law system reflects the interpretation and legal organization of rabbinic Judaism.

Nearly two thousand years after the emergence of the early rabbinic tradition, that framework is now being used to establish an international religious movement, complete with its own institutions, governing authorities, and declared prophetic purpose.

Its organizers have chosen Jerusalem as the place to begin.

The Movement Gathering in Jerusalem

The Noahide World Center presents itself as an institution dedicated to teaching the universal Torah to the nations. Its spiritual leader is Rabbi Oury Cherki, and its activities include religious education, community organization, and guidance for non-Jews who accept the Noahide commandments.

Its planned November congress marks a more ambitious stage of that work.

The official announcement is titled World Noahide Congress 2026. Beneath the title appears a promise that participants will stand where history begins anew.

The organizers then quote Zechariah 2:15, corresponding to Zechariah 2:11 in many English editions, concerning the nations joining themselves to the Lord.

Those four words reveal how the organizers understand their gathering. They are identifying the planned congress with Zechariah’s prophecy concerning the nations joining themselves to the Lord, presenting their movement as part of its fulfillment.

The organizers continue:

“For two thousand years, the prophet’s words waited. We waited.”

Zechariah lived centuries before the birth of Christ. The prophecy’s age is therefore greater than the two thousand years invoked in the announcement. The wording nevertheless reveals how the movement understands its present mission: a long-awaited gathering of the nations is now taking institutional form.

The congress program provides the details.

Its proposed foundations include a signed charter, a unified religious syllabus, regional councils, financial infrastructure, and an international Beit Din.

Participants are being invited to establish a movement intended to continue long after the gathering ends.

The organizers make clear where religious authority within this new structure will reside.

Among the organization’s five pillars is:

“Authority - Guidance rooted in the sages of Israel, not improvised alone.”

This is the point at which the ancient Noahide commandments and the modern institution meet.

The movement does not simply ask non-Jews to acknowledge the Creator and live according to basic moral principles. It proposes a religious identity formed through rabbinic teaching, structured membership, religious observances, and recognized institutions.

The organization’s educational material explains that formal acceptance of the Noahide commandments can involve appearing before a Jewish Beit Din, acknowledging the commandments as divine obligations transmitted through the Torah and interpreted within rabbinic tradition.

The proposed international Beit Din would give this religious framework a central institution in Jerusalem, operating alongside the regional councils and unified educational system.

The organizers also announce a reception at Beit HaNasi, the Israeli President’s Residence. Their website presents this as recognition at the highest level of the State of Israel.

The direction is clear from the organization’s own documents. The Noahide World Center intends to unite communities across six continents under a common religious identity, with Jerusalem as their spiritual center and the sages of Israel providing religious guidance.

But the most consequential claim concerns prophecy.

The organizers have taken Zechariah’s promise that the nations will join themselves to the Lord and declared that their gathering marks its fulfillment.

“This is that day.”

To understand the weight of those words, we must return to the prophets themselves, and then examine how Jesus Christ and His apostles understood the nations coming to God.

When the Prophets Spoke of the Nations

The organizers are correct about one essential point: the prophets did foresee the nations turning toward the God of Israel.

Isaiah describes the mountain of the Lord being exalted and the nations coming to receive His instruction.

“And many nations shall go and say, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will tell us his way, and we will walk in it: for out of Sion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord out of Jerusalem.”- Isaiah 2:3

The prophecy concerns far more than Israel’s national life. The nations themselves are drawn toward the Lord.

Zechariah develops this expectation further. His prophecy describes many nations joining themselves to God and becoming His people.

The Noahide World Center places this prophecy at the heart of its mission, presenting the gathering of the nations under rabbinic guidance as its fulfillment.

Yet Scripture carries the account further. The Gospels identify Jesus Christ as the promised Messiah, and the apostles proclaim how God’s promises to the nations are fulfilled through Him.

The prophets foretold that the nations would come to the God of Israel. Christ revealed the way, and the apostles carried that message beyond Jerusalem to the nations themselves.

What Jesus Said About the Nations

After His resurrection, Jesus gives His apostles a commission extending far beyond the borders of Israel.

“Having gone therefore, disciple all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”- Matthew 28:19

The nations are to become disciples of Jesus Christ.

The commission continues in Matthew 28:20 with the instruction to teach them to observe everything He commanded.

Here the Christian mission is established directly by Christ. The apostles are sent to the nations with His teaching and His authority.

Earlier, Jesus had already declared:

“I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.”- John 14:6

These words establish the foundation of the Christian understanding of access to God.

Jesus does not direct the nations toward a separate religious order administered by the sages. He identifies Himself as the way to the Father.

The apostles understood the implications.

When the first Gentiles began entering the Church, the question of their obligations became a serious dispute among the believers.

Some insisted that Gentile converts must be circumcised and observe the Law of Moses.

The dispute was brought before the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, the ancient city where Jesus had been crucified and raised from the dead, and where the Church first began proclaiming His resurrection.

Their decision is recorded in Acts 15.

James instructed that Gentile believers should abstain from the pollutions of idols, sexual immorality, what is strangled, and blood.

The resemblance to several Noahide principles is evident. Both traditions address idolatry, sexual conduct, and blood.

Yet Acts 15 does not establish the later seven-law system as the religious identity of Gentile Christians. The council addresses Gentile believers who have already turned to God through Jesus Christ.

Peter states the principle at the heart of the decision:

“But we believe ourselves to be saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same manner as they also.” - Acts 15:11

Jew and Gentile receive salvation through the same Lord, Jesus Christ. The apostles establish one way of reconciliation with God, regardless of a person’s ancestry or former standing under the Law.

Paul explains this further in his letter to the Ephesians. He reminds Gentile believers that they were once strangers to the covenants of promise, separated from the commonwealth of Israel and without hope in the world.

Then he declares what changed through Christ.

“But now in Christ Jesus you, the ones once being far off, have become near by the blood of Christ.” - Ephesians 2:13

Paul goes further, declaring that Christ has broken down the division between Jew and Gentile, reconciling both to God through His sacrifice.

In Ephesians 2:18, he establishes that both now have access to the Father through Christ, in one Spirit. The nations once described as strangers to the covenants are brought near through the Messiah Himself.

Their place among God’s people rests upon Christ and what He accomplished, not upon ancestry or submission to a separate religious authority.

Paul makes this even clearer in his letter to the Galatians:

“And if you are of Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise.” - Galatians 3:29

The promise to Abraham reaches the nations through belonging to Jesus Christ.

That is how the apostles understood the fulfillment of God’s promises.

The Question Jerusalem Must Answer

In November 2026, the Noahide World Center intends to gather representatives from across the world in Jerusalem. Its leaders speak of prophecy, covenant, religious authority, and the nations joining themselves to God.

The proposed charter, religious court, and regional councils are intended to turn that vision into a lasting international institution.

To understand what is taking shape in Jerusalem, we must distinguish the biblical foundations from the religious system built upon them.

God’s covenant with Noah is recorded in Genesis. Scripture condemns murder, theft, idolatry, and sexual immorality, while Jubilees preserves Noah’s instructions to his descendants concerning righteousness and obedience to God.

Rabbinic Judaism later organized these commandments into a seven-law framework for the nations, drawing upon Scripture through its own methods of interpretation. The modern Noahide movement has taken that framework and made it the foundation of a distinct religious identity, complete with organized membership, rabbinic guidance, and international institutions.

The organizers now present this movement as part of the fulfillment of biblical prophecy, declaring that the nations are gathering in Jerusalem to join themselves to the God of Israel.

But the apostles already proclaimed how the nations would come to the God of Israel.

The nations were called to God through His Son.

Peter announced Him to Israel. Paul carried His Gospel to the Gentiles. The apostles taught that the promises of God were being fulfilled through the crucified and risen Messiah.

The distinction reaches the very heart of Christianity.

The Noahide movement directs non-Jews toward the universal Torah under rabbinic guidance. The Gospel directs the nations toward the Son of God, through whom they receive access to the Father.

And when the apostles were questioned about the way of salvation, Peter gave an answer that leaves little room for competing religious authorities:

“And there is salvation in no one else, for neither is there another name under heaven having been given among men by which it behooves us to be saved.” - Acts 4:12

The prophets promised that the nations would come to the Lord.

The apostles proclaimed the name through which they would come.

Jesus Christ.

Continue the Investigation

The history of Scripture, religious authority, and the nations extends far beyond the Noahide movement. Kingdom Code examines these questions through Scripture, ancient witnesses, and the traditions that shaped Christianity.
